Ruth — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

This book gives excellent examples of faith, devotion to God, patience, humility, diligence and loving-kindness in the ordinary events of life.

It also shows how carefully God's providence attends to even our smallest concerns.

That should encourage us to place our full trust in him.

We may read Ruth as a beautiful and natural picture of human life, as a detailed record of important events, and as part of God's plan of redemption.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesElimelech and his sons die in the land of Moab.1–5Naomi returns home.6–14Orpah stays behind, but Ruth goes with Naomi.15–18They come to Bethlehem.19–22
Elimelech's family in Moab (verses 1–5)

Elimelech was not wrong to care about providing for his family.

But Henry says his decision to move to Moab cannot be justified.

The move ended with the loss of his family.

It is foolish to imagine we can escape a hardship that God has placed in our path and calls us to bear.

Moving somewhere else seldom improves our spiritual situation.

We do not know what may happen when we bring young people into harmful company and remove them from public worship.

We may think their religious foundations are strong and that they are well prepared to resist temptation.

Yet we cannot see the outcome.

The text does not say that the Moabite women whom Elimelech's sons married had converted to Israel's faith.

All earthly trials and pleasures last only a short time.

Death continually removes people of every age and condition, undoing our worldly comforts.

We should therefore value most highly the good things that endure forever.

Naomi decides to return (verses 6–14)

After the deaths of her sons, Naomi began planning to return home.

When death enters a family, the survivors should consider what needs changing in their lives.

God sometimes allows earthly life to become bitter so that heaven becomes more precious to us.

Naomi appears to have been a woman of faith and devotion.

She said goodbye to her daughters-in-law with prayer.

Friends should part in love and prayer.

Was Naomi right to discourage them from accompanying her, when going with her might help them escape Moab's idolatry and worship Israel's God?

Henry says Naomi certainly wanted that good outcome, but she did not want them to adopt Israel's religion only to please her.

People who profess faith merely to satisfy friends or enjoy their company make unreliable converts.

If they accompanied Naomi, they should make a considered, personal decision, understanding its cost.

Anyone professing faith should count the cost first.

Many people prefer the earthly rest of marriage, financial security or comfortable circumstances to the rest Christ offers their souls.

When their loyalty is tested, they may leave Christ, perhaps with real sorrow.

Orpah stays; Ruth follows Naomi (verses 15–18)

Consider Ruth's determination and genuine love for Naomi.

Orpah was distressed at parting, but she did not love Naomi enough to leave Moab for her sake.

Similarly, many people value Christ and feel affection toward him, yet fail to receive his salvation because they will not give up other things for him.

They love him in a sense, but leave him because they love something else more.

Ruth is an example of God's grace moving a soul to choose the better portion.

Naomi could ask for nothing more than Ruth's solemn declaration.

A firm resolution is powerful against temptation.

When someone follows a religious path without a settled decision, that person is like a half-open door inviting a thief.

A determined heart closes and bolts the door, resists the devil and causes him to flee.

Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem (verses 19–22)

They came to Bethlehem.

Suffering can change a person's situation very quickly and dramatically.

May God's grace prepare us for every such change, especially the greatest change of all.

Naomi means pleasant or lovable.

Mara means bitter or bitterness.

Naomi felt that sorrow described her life.

She returned home empty: poor, widowed and without children.

But believers possess a fullness no hardship can empty, a good portion that cannot be taken away.

Suffering is a bitter cup.

Naomi acknowledged that hers had come under God's providence.

When the Lord humbles us through our circumstances, we should humble our hearts before him.

Suffering is not beneficial merely because it hurts; it does us good when we respond to it rightly.
classic_reading:
[Ruth.1.1-Ruth.1.5]
Ruth
We find in this book excellent examples of faith, piety, patience, humility, industry, and loving-kindness, in the common events of life. Also we see the special care which God's providence take of our smallest concerns, encouraging us to full trust therein. We may view this book as a beautiful, because natural representation of human life; as a curious detail of important facts; and as a part of the plan of redemption.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
Elimelech and his sons die in the land of Moab. | (1-5) |
Naomi returns home. | (6-14) |
Orpah stays behind, but Ruth goes with Naomi. | (15-18) |
They come to Bethlehem. | (19-22) |
Verses 1-5
Elimelech's care to provide for his family, was not to be blamed; but his removal into the country of Moab could not be justified. And the removal ended in the wasting of his family. It is folly to think of escaping that cross, which, being laid in our way, we ought to take up. Changing our place seldom is mending it. Those who bring young people into bad acquaintance, and take them out of the way of public ordinances, thought they may think them well-principled, and armed against temptation, know not what will be the end. It does not appear that the women the sons of Elimelech married, were proselyted to the Jewish religion. Earthly trials or enjoyments are of short continuance. Death continually removes those of every age and situation, and mars all our outward comforts: we cannot too strongly prefer those advantages which shall last for ever.
[Ruth.1.6-Ruth.1.14]
Verses 6-14
Naomi began to think of returning, after the death of her two sons. When death comes into a family, it ought to reform what is amiss there. Earth is made bitter to us, that heaven may be made dear. Naomi seems to have been a person of faith and piety. She dismissed her daughters-in-law with prayer. It is very proper for friends, when they part, to part with them thus part in love. Did Naomi do well, to discourage her daughters from going with her, when she might save them from the idolatry of Moab, and bring them to the faith and worship of the God of Israel? Naomi, no doubt, desired to do that; but if they went with her, she would not have them to go upon her account. Those that take upon them a profession of religion only to oblige their friends, or for the sake of company, will be converts of small value. If they did come with her, she would have them make it their deliberate choice, and sit down first and count the cost, as it concerns those to do who make a profession of religion. And more desire "rest in the house of a husband," or some wordly settlement or earthly satisfaction, than the rest to which Christ invites our souls; therefore when tried they will depart from Christ, though perhaps with some sorrow.
[Ruth.1.15-Ruth.1.18]
Verses 15-18
See Ruth's resolution, and her good affection to Naomi. Orpah was loth to part from her; yet she did not love her well enough to leave Moab for her sake. Thus, many have a value and affection for Christ, yet come short of salvation by him, because they will not forsake other things for him. They love him, yet leave him, because they do not love him enough, but love other things better. Ruth is an example of the grace of God, inclining the soul to choose the better part. Naomi could desire no more than the solemn declaration Ruth made. See the power of resolution; it silences temptation. Those that go in religious ways without a stedfast mind, stand like a door half open, which invites a thief; but resolution shuts and bolts the door, resists the devil and forces him to flee.
[Ruth.1.19-Ruth.1.22]
Verses 19-22
Naomi and Ruth came to Bethlehem. Afflictions will make great and surprising changes in a little time. May God, by his grace, fit us for all such changes, especially the great change!, Naomi signifies "pleasant," or "amiable;" Mara, "bitter," or "bitterness." She was now a woman of a sorrowful spirit. She had come home empty, poor, a widow and childless. But there is a fulness for believers of which they never can be emptied; a good part which shall not be taken from those who have it. The cup of affliction is a "bitter" cup, but she owns that the affliction came from God. It well becomes us to have our hearts humbled under humbling providences. It is not affliction itself, but affliction rightly borne, that does us good.

Ruth goes to glean in Boaz's field (verses 1–3)

Notice Ruth's humility.

When Providence made her poor, she accepted her circumstances cheerfully.

Proud people might rather starve than take a humble position.

Ruth was different.

She herself proposed gathering leftover grain.

She asked permission with modesty.

We should not demand another person's kindness as though it were owed to us, but ask for it and accept it gratefully, even in small matters.

Ruth was also diligent.

She had no desire to eat the food of idleness.

Her example is especially valuable for young people.

Diligence promises good both for this life and for the next.

We must not be ashamed of any honest work.

No lawful occupation is beneath us.

Sin should be beneath us; nothing else is shameful when Providence calls us to it.

Ruth also cared for her mother-in-law and trusted in God.

The Lord wisely orders even events that seem unimportant or uncertain, directing them to his glory and the good of his people.

Boaz treats Ruth kindly (verses 4–16)

The godly, kindly words exchanged between Boaz and his workers show that there were faithful people in Israel.

How different this was from the immoral and corrupt speech heard too often in workplaces!

A stranger who heard them would gain a very different impression of Israel from what someone might gather from the careless speech common elsewhere.

Genuine faith teaches people to behave rightly whatever their social position.

It produces kind employers, faithful workers and harmony within households.

It fosters love and kindness between people of different ranks.

Boaz prayed for his workers when he arrived.

They replied with respect rather than speaking bitterly about him as soon as he was gone.

Relationships work well where employers and workers share such goodwill.

They expressed kindness by praying for one another.

Boaz noticed the unfamiliar woman and ordered that she be treated well.

Employers must ensure not only that they themselves do no wrong but also that people under their authority do not mistreat others.

Ruth humbly acknowledged that she had no right to expect these favors, having been born and raised among pagans.

We should all think humbly of ourselves, regarding others as worthy of honor.

Boaz's kindness toward poor Ruth also points to the Lord Jesus Christ's kindness toward needy sinners.

Ruth returns with the grain she gathered (verses 17–23)

Even humble work like gleaning produces something useful.

This should encourage diligence.

Ruth valued what her hard work had obtained and took care to preserve it.

We should likewise guard against losing the spiritual good we have worked for (2 John 1:8).

Parents should ask children about their daily activities as Naomi did.

They should not question them so harshly that they dread being home or feel tempted to lie.

Instead, they should praise what is good and gently correct or caution them when needed.

Each evening we should ask ourselves: Where have I gleaned today?

Have I grown in knowledge and grace?

What have I done that will bear lasting good fruit?

When the Lord deals generously with us, let us not search for happiness or satisfaction in another field.

We lose divine favors when we treat them lightly.

Ruth carefully followed Naomi's instructions.

When the harvest ended, she stayed home to keep her elderly mother-in-law company.

Dinah once went out merely to visit the daughters of the land, and her vanity ended in shame (Genesis 34).

Ruth went out only to obtain food and help provide for Naomi.

Her humility and hard work finally led to honor.

[Ruth.2.1-Ruth.2.3]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz. | (1-3) |
The kindness of Boaz to Ruth. | (4-16) |
Ruth returns to her mother-in-law.
(17-23)
Verses 1-3
Observe Ruth's humility. When Providence had made her poor, she cheerfully stoops to her lot. High spirits will rather starve than stoop; not so Ruth. Nay, it is her own proposal. She speaks humbly in her expectation of leave to glean. We may not demand kindness as a debt, but ask, and take it as a favour, though in a small matter. Ruth also was an example of industry. She loved not to eat the bread of idleness. This is an example to young people. Diligence promises well, both for this world and the other. We must not be shy of any honest employment. No labour is a reproach. Sin is a thing below us, but we must not think any thing else so, to which Providence call us. She was an example of regard to her mother, and of trust in Providence. God wisely orders what seem to us small events; and those that appear altogether uncertain, still are directed to serve his own glory, and the good of his people.
[Ruth.2.4-Ruth.2.16]
Verses 4-16
The pious and kind language between Boaz and his reapers shows that there were godly persons in Israel. Such language as this is seldom heard in our field; too often, on the contrary, what is immoral and corrupt. A stranger would form a very different opinion of our land, from that which Ruth would form of Israel from the converse and conduct of Boaz and his reapers. But true religion will teach a man to behave aright in all states and conditions; it will form kind masters and faithful servants, and cause harmony in families. True religion will cause mutual love and kindness among persons of different ranks. It had these effects on Boaz and his men. When he came to them he prayed for them. They did not, as soon as he was out of hearing curse him, as some ill-natured servants that hate their master's eye, but they returned his courtesy. Things are likely to go on well where there is such good-will as this between masters and servants. They expressed their kindness to each other by praying one for another. Boaz inquired concerning the stranger he saw, and ordered her to be well treated. Masters must take care, not only that they do no hurt themselves, but that they suffer not their servants and those under them to do wrong. Ruth humbly owned herself unworthy of favours, seeing she was born and brought up a heathen. It well becomes us all to think humbly of ourselves, esteeming others better than ourselves. And let us, in the kindness of Boaz to Ruth, note the kindness of the Lord Jesus Christ to poor sinners.
[Ruth.2.17-Ruth.2.23]
Verses 17-23
It encourages industry, that in all labour, even that of gleaning, there is profit. Ruth was pleased with what she gained by her own industry, and was careful to secure it. Let us thus take care that we lose not those things which we have wrought, which we have gained for our souls' good, [2John.1.8] 2Jo 1:8. Parents should examine their children, as Naomi did, not to frighten or discourage them, so as to make them hate home, or tempt them to tell a lie; but to commend them if they have done well, and with mildness to reprove and caution them if they have done otherwise. It is a good question for us to ask ourselves every night, Where have I gleaned to-day? What improvement have I made in knowledge and grace? What have I done that will turn to a good account? When the Lord deals bountifully with us, let us not be found in any other field, nor seeking for happiness and satisfaction in the creature. We lose Divine favours, if we slight them. Ruth dutifully observed her mother's directions. And when the harvest was ended, she kept her aged mother company at home. Dinah went out to see the daughters of the land; her vanity ended in disgrace, Ge 34. Ruth kept at home, and helped to maintain her mother, and went out on no other errand than to get provision for her; her humility and industry ended in preferment.

Naomi advises Ruth about marriage (verses 1–5)

Marriage ought to provide as much lasting rest and security as anything can provide in this world.

It should establish a lifelong relationship and settle a person's affections.

That is why marriage should be entered into seriously, with earnest prayers for God's guidance and blessing and with careful attention to his commands.

Parents should advise their children thoughtfully on this important matter, seeking their spiritual good.

Always remember: what is best for us is what is best for our souls.

Naomi's advice may seem strange to modern readers, but it reflected the laws and customs of Israel.

Henry argues that Naomi would not have recommended it if the action had carried the appearance of wrongdoing.

Ruth had now joined the true faith.

The laws and customs of Israel gave her a legal claim involving Boaz as a possible family redeemer.

Widows customarily asserted such claims (Deuteronomy 25:5–10).

But this conduct is not recorded for imitation in other times, nor should it be judged as though the ancient custom were the same as today's.

Had the proposal been wrong, Henry believes Ruth's virtue and good judgment would have led her to refuse it.

Boaz responds to Ruth's request (verses 6–13)

Something improper in one country or period is not necessarily improper in another.

Boaz, as a judge of Israel, could explain what Ruth should do.

He could also determine whether he possessed the right of redemption and what steps and ceremonies were necessary for marriage to him or to another relative.

His conduct deserves the greatest praise.

He did not exploit Ruth or treat her with contempt because she was a poor foreign widow.

Nor did he suspect her of evil intentions.

He spoke respectfully of her as a virtuous woman and made her a promise.

As soon as morning came, he sent her away with a gift for Naomi.

Boaz's promise was conditional: a nearer relative had the first right of redemption.

Ruth returns home to Naomi (verses 14–18)

Ruth had done everything appropriate for her to do.

Now she needed to wait patiently for the result.

Boaz had accepted responsibility and would deal with the matter carefully.

Believers have even stronger reason to entrust their worries to God, because he has promised to care for them.

Our strength may sometimes be to remain quiet and wait (Isaiah 30:7).

This history encourages us to come by faith to the feet of Jesus Christ.

He is our close Relative, having taken our human nature.

He possesses the right to redeem us.

We should seek his guidance and ask, “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6).

Christ will never condemn us for asking him such a question.

Let us also desire and seek this same spiritual rest for our children and friends, so that all may be well with them.

[Ruth.3.1-Ruth.3.5]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The directions given to Ruth by Naomi. | (1-5) |
Boaz acknowledges the duty of a kinsman. | (6-13) |
Ruth's return to her mother-in-law.
(14-18)
Verses 1-5
The married state should be a rest, as much as any thing upon earth can be so, as it ought to fix the affections and form a connexion for life. Therefore it should be engaged in with great seriousness, with earnest prayers for direction, for the blessing of God, and with regard to his precepts. Parents should carefully advise their children in this important concern, that it may be well with them as to their souls. Be it always remembered, That is best for us which is best for our souls. The course Naomi advised appears strange to us; but it was according to the laws and usages of Israel. If the proposed measure had borne the appearance of evil, Naomi would not have advised it. Law and custom gave Ruth, who was now proselyted to the true religion, a legal claim upon Boaz. It was customary for widows to assert this claim, [Deut.25.5-Deut.25.10] De 25:5-10. But this is not recorded for imitation in other times, and is not to be judged by modern rules. And if there had been any evil in it, Ruth was a woman of too much virtue and too much sense to have listened to it.
[Ruth.3.6-Ruth.3.13]
Verses 6-13
What in one age or nation would be improper, is not always so in another age or another nation. Being a judge of Israel, Boaz would tell Ruth what she should do; also whether he had the right of redemption, and what methods must be taken, and what rites used, in order to accomplishing her marriage with him or another person. The conduct of Boaz calls for the highest praise. He attempted not to take advantage of Ruth; he did not disdain her as a poor, destitute stranger, nor suspect her of any ill intentions. He spoke honourably of her as a virtuous woman, made her a promise, and as soon as the morning arrived, sent her away with a present to her mother-in-law. Boaz made his promise conditional, for there was a kinsman nearer than he, to whom the right of redemption belonged.
[Ruth.3.14-Ruth.3.18]
Verses 14-18
Ruth had done all that was fit for her to do, she must patiently wait the event. Boaz, having undertaken this matter, would be sure to manage it well. Much more reason have true believers to cast their care on God, because he has promised to care for them. Our strength is to sit still, [Isa.30.7] Is 30:7. This narrative may encourage us to lay ourselves by faith at the feet of Christ: He is our near Kinsman; having taken our nature upon him. He has the right to redeem. Let us seek to receive from him his directions: Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? [Acts.9.6] Ac 9:6. He will never blame us as doing this unseasonably. And let us earnestly desire and seek the same rest for our children and friends, that it may be well with them also.

The nearer relative declines redemption (verses 1–8)

The matter was governed by the laws Moses had given about family inheritances.

Henry assumes it was settled openly and according to the required legal procedures.

When the nearer relative heard all the conditions, he refused to redeem the property.

Many people respond similarly when presented with the great redemption offered by God.

They have heard good things about faith.

They have no particular criticism of it.

They may even speak respectfully of it.

But they remain unwilling to commit themselves, because they fear that doing so will reduce their worldly wealth or opportunities.

The nearer relative therefore surrendered his right to Boaz.

Everyone who desires to be a genuine Israelite, without deceit, must act with honesty and fairness in contracts and trade.

In the end, honest dealings prove the wisest policy.

Boaz takes Ruth as his wife (verses 9–12)

People are quick to seize chances to enlarge their estates.

Yet few recognize how precious true devotion to God is.

The world calls some people wise whom the Lord calls foolish.

They neglect their souls and reject Christ's salvation because they fear losing earthly advantage.

God, however, honored Boaz by making him part of the Messiah's family line.

The other relative, who worried about reducing his property and position, is forgotten.

His name, family and inheritance have disappeared from the record.

Ruth gives birth to Obed (verses 13–22)

Ruth bore a son, through whose descendants thousands upon thousands would belong to God.

As a direct ancestor of Jesus Christ, she played a part in bringing blessing to everyone who would be saved through him.

That included Gentiles as well as Jews.

Ruth's story was a witness to the Gentile world that God had not abandoned its peoples forever.

In due time they would become one with his chosen people and share in his salvation.

Prayer accompanied the marriage, and praise accompanied the birth of the child.

How sad that such expressions of faith are uncommon among Christians—or become empty formalities!

This passage also traces David's descent from Ruth.

The time eventually came when Bethlehem in Judah witnessed wonders far greater than those recorded in her story.

There, another child was born in humble circumstances.

His birth affected the decrees of the Roman ruler of the world.

It brought princes and wise men from the east to his feet, carrying gold, frankincense and myrrh.

His name will endure forever.

All nations will call him blessed.

In that promised Offspring, all the nations of the earth will receive blessing.

[Ruth.4.1-Ruth.4.8]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
The kinsman refuses to redeem Ruth's inheritance. | (1-8) |
Boaz marries Ruth. | (9-12) |
Birth of Obed. | (13-22) |
Verses 1-8
This matter depended on the laws given by Moses about inheritances, and doubtless the whole was settled in the regular and legal manner. This kinsman, when he heard the conditions of the bargain, refused it. In like manner many are shy of the great redemption; they are not willing to espouse religion; they have heard well of it, and have nothing to say against it; they will give it their good word, but they are willing to part with it, and cannot be bound to it, for fear of marring their own inheritance in this world. The right was resigned to Boaz. Fair and open dealing in all matters of contract and trade, is what all must make conscience of, who would approve themselves true Israelites, without guile. Honesty will be found the best policy.
[Ruth.4.9-Ruth.4.12]
Verses 9-12
Men are ready to seize opportunities for increasing their estates, but few know the value of godliness. Such are the wise men of this world, whom the Lord charges with folly. They attend not to the concerns of their souls, but reject the salvation of Christ, for fear of marring their inheritance. But God did Boaz the honour to bring him into the line of the Messiah, while the kinsman, who was afraid of lessening himself, and marring his inheritance, has his name, family, and inheritance forgotten.
[Ruth.4.13-Ruth.4.22]
Verses 13-22
Ruth bore a son, through whom thousands and myriads were born to God; and in being the lineal ancestor of Christ, she was instrumental in the happiness of all that shall be saved by him; even of us Gentiles, as well as those of Jewish descent. She was a witness for God to the Gentile world, that he had not utterly forsaken them, but that in due time they should become one with his chosen people, and partake of his salvation. Prayer to God attended the marriage, and praise to him attended the birth of the child. What a pity it is that pious language should not be more used among Christians, or that it should be let fall into formality! Here is the descent of David from Ruth. And the period came when Bethlehem-Judah displayed greater wonders than those in the history of Ruth, when the outcast babe of another forlorn female of the same race appeared, controlling the counsels of the Roman master of the world, and drawing princes and wise men from the east, with treasures of gold, and frankincense, and myrrh to his feet. His name shall endure for ever, and all nations shall call Him blessed. In that Seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed.
